parts.title: Ordering a photo book
parts.context: A man orders a photo book as an anniversary present.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a man phoning a print shop to order a photo book. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: callie
script.text: PixelPrint, Callie speaking.

script.speaker: dan
script.text: Hello. I'd like to order a photo book, please. It's a present for my parents' wedding anniversary, and I want to surprise them.

script.speaker: callie
script.text: What a lovely idea. I'll take some details.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The book is an anniversary present, so 'anniversary' has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: callie
script.text: Could I have your name, please?

script.speaker: dan
script.text: Dan Fletcher. That's F-L-E-T-C-H-E-R.

script.speaker: callie
script.text: Thank you, Mr Fletcher. How many photographs do you want in the book?

script.speaker: dan
script.text: About eighty. I thought a hundred at first, but I couldn't find that many good ones.

script.speaker: callie
script.text: Eighty is plenty. What size would you like? We have A4, A5 and a large square format.

script.speaker: dan
script.text: The square one, I think. It's more unusual.

script.speaker: callie
script.text: Good choice. Would you like a soft cover or a hard cover?

script.speaker: dan
script.text: A hard cover, so that it lasts.

script.speaker: callie
script.text: And the paper? We offer glossy or matt.

script.speaker: dan
script.text: Matt, please. Glossy paper shows every fingerprint.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: callie
script.text: That comes to forty-five pounds. It would have been fifty-five with the glossy paper, but the matt is cheaper.

script.speaker: dan
script.text: That's fine. How long will it take?

script.speaker: callie
script.text: Delivery takes five working days, so you'll need to order by next Monday if you want it for the weekend.

script.speaker: dan
script.text: That's cutting it fine. Do I need to send the photographs on a disc?

script.speaker: callie
script.text: No, you can upload them from your phone, or from your computer. The software will help you arrange them on the pages.

script.speaker: dan
script.text: Can I put something on the cover?

script.speaker: callie
script.text: Yes, a personal message, up to fifty characters. A lot of people put their names and the date.

script.speaker: dan
script.text: I'll do that. Is there anything cheaper?

script.speaker: callie
script.text: If you order before Friday, we'll give you free delivery, which saves you four pounds. Shall I make a note?

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A photography exhibition
parts.context: A curator introduces an exhibition at a gallery.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear a gallery guide introducing a photography exhibition. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: quinn
script.text: Welcome to the Lakeside Gallery, and to this year's photography exhibition. I'm Fiona Quinn, the curator. Please look at your plan. We're at the entrance, at the bottom, and the path takes you straight up to the main corridor.

script.speaker: quinn
script.text: The rooms along the top are the main exhibition. From left to right, the first room is the portraits. Next to it, the landscapes. In the middle, the black-and-white room, which many visitors find the most moving. And at the far right, the wildlife room.

script.speaker: quinn
script.text: Below the corridor, on the left of the entrance path, is the street photography room. On the right of the path is the café, and at the far right, the shop.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: quinn
script.text: A few facts. About three hundred photographs are on display, chosen from more than two thousand submitted by photographers from forty countries.

script.speaker: quinn
script.text: The theme of this year's exhibition is home. We asked photographers to show what home means to them, and you'll see everything from city flats to tents in the desert.

script.speaker: quinn
script.text: You might notice that the photographs are not behind glass. That's deliberate, because glass causes reflections, and we want you to see the images clearly. Please don't touch them, though, and don't use a flash.

script.speaker: quinn
script.text: On Thursday evenings, the café hosts a talk by one of the photographers. They explain how a picture was taken, and you can ask questions. It's free with your ticket.

script.speaker: quinn
script.text: Tickets are eight pounds, but students pay four, and children under twelve go free. Please enjoy the exhibition, and do ask the staff if you have any questions.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Teenagers and social media
parts.context: Two sociology students discuss the results of their study.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two sociology students, Lydia and Omar, discussing their study of teenagers and social media. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: lydia
script.text: Omar, I've finished transcribing the interviews. We spoke to thirty teenagers in all, didn't we?

script.speaker: omar
script.text: Yes, between thirteen and sixteen years old, from two schools. We wanted more, but it took longer than expected to get permission.

script.speaker: lydia
script.text: How did we find them? I can't remember.

script.speaker: omar
script.text: They were volunteers. The teachers told their classes about the study, and anyone who was interested gave us their name.

script.speaker: lydia
script.text: That could be a weakness. People who volunteer may be more confident than the others, so it's something to mention.

script.speaker: omar
script.text: How long did each interview last?

script.speaker: lydia
script.text: About twenty minutes. Ten would have been too short, and forty-five would have bored them.

script.speaker: omar
script.text: What surprised you most?

script.speaker: lydia
script.text: That most of them said they spent about three hours a day online, but when we checked the usage data on their phones, it was often more than that.

script.speaker: omar
script.text: Our tutor will want us to present the results in a clear way.

script.speaker: lydia
script.text: A short written report, I think. A poster wouldn't have enough space for the quotations.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: lydia
script.text: Let's summarise what they said about each platform. The photo app first.

script.speaker: omar
script.text: Many of the girls said it made them feel anxious, because they compared themselves with other people's pictures.

script.speaker: lydia
script.text: The video app?

script.speaker: omar
script.text: Nearly all of them said it takes up too much time. They start watching one clip, and an hour later they're still there.

script.speaker: lydia
script.text: The messaging app?

script.speaker: omar
script.text: That was positive. They use it to keep in touch with family, especially relatives who live abroad.

script.speaker: lydia
script.text: The discussion forum?

script.speaker: omar
script.text: A few older students said it helps their studies, because they can ask questions about homework.

script.speaker: lydia
script.text: And the gaming platform?

script.speaker: omar
script.text: They said it makes them feel connected with friends, even when they can't meet in person. Shall I write the first draft?

script.speaker: lydia
script.text: Yes, please. I'll prepare the tables.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: how stars are born and die
parts.context: An astronomy lecture on the life cycle of stars.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about how stars are born and die. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Good afternoon. Today's lecture is about the life cycle of stars, from birth to death, and what that means for us.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Stars are born in huge clouds of gas and dust called nebulae. Within such a cloud, a dense region starts to collapse, because gravity pulls the material together, and as it contracts, it heats up. When the centre becomes hot enough, nuclear fusion begins, in which hydrogen is turned into helium, and a star is born. This process releases the energy that makes the star shine.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: A star spends most of its life in a stable state, in which the pressure from the fusion balances the pull of gravity. Our own Sun has been in this state for about four and a half billion years, and it will last for about ten billion years in all.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: When the hydrogen in the core runs out, the star's life changes. A star like the Sun swells enormously, and becomes a red giant. Eventually, it sheds its outer layers into space, and what remains is a small, hot core called a white dwarf, which slowly cools over billions of years.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The story is more dramatic for stars much bigger than the Sun. Their cores collapse in a fraction of a second, and the star explodes in what is called a supernova, which can briefly outshine a whole galaxy. What is left behind may be an extremely dense neutron star, or, if the star was massive enough, a black hole.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Why does this matter to us? Because stars are factories. In the early universe there were only hydrogen and helium. Elements such as carbon and oxygen were made inside stars, and then scattered into space when they died. The explosions spread this material, and eventually it formed new stars, planets and, in our case, living things. We are all, quite literally, made from the remains of stars. Next week we'll look at galaxies.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.
